objectives: Recognize classic occupational toxicology cases: silica, asbestos, lead, mercury.
Apply TLV-TWA + PEL + REL + STEL + biomonitoring + Bradford Hill criteria.
Implement the hazard-control hierarchy from elimination through PPE.

slides.title: Classic workplace exposures: silica, asbestos, lead, mercury
slides.body:
**Occupational toxicology** is the application of toxicology to workplace exposures. Workers experience the highest doses of most industrial chemicals + were historically the population in whom toxicity was first recognized. Classic cohort findings drove much of modern toxicology + chemical regulation.

**Silica + silicosis**:
- **Crystalline silica (SiO₂, quartz, cristobalite, tridymite)** — ubiquitous in mining, quarrying, sandblasting, tunneling, foundries, ceramics, glass, stoneworking, hydraulic fracturing (frac sand), engineered-stone countertop fabrication.
- **Silicosis** — chronic + accelerated + acute forms; fibrotic lung disease from alveolar macrophage uptake of inhaled silica → lysosomal damage + inflammasome activation (NLRP3) → progressive massive fibrosis + lung-function loss. Acute silicosis (proteinosis pattern) develops in months of intense exposure; chronic over decades. Latency 10-30 yr.
- **Hawks Nest Tunnel disaster (1930-1932, West Virginia)** — Union Carbide subsidiary tunneling project through nearly-pure silica rock at Gauley Bridge; ~3000 workers (most Black, migrant); estimated 700+ deaths from acute silicosis within 5 years — the worst industrial disaster in US history. Documented by Muriel Rukeyser's *The Book of the Dead* (1938). Spurred OSHA establishment + the modern silica standard.
- Engineered-stone (artificial quartz countertops, ~93% silica) workers experiencing a renewed silicosis epidemic 2010s+; high silica exposure + young workers.
- Silica + tuberculosis: silicotic lungs are highly susceptible to TB (silicotuberculosis).
- IARC Group 1 carcinogen — lung cancer.
- **OSHA silica standard (2016)** — PEL 50 μg/m³ TWA + Action Level 25 μg/m³; required engineering controls + medical surveillance + respiratory protection.

**Asbestos + mesothelioma + asbestosis**:
- **Asbestos** — six naturally-occurring fibrous silicate minerals; major commercial forms chrysotile (white, serpentine; >90% of historical use) + amphiboles (crocidolite blue, amosite brown). Used in insulation, fireproofing, brake pads, roofing, shipbuilding, cement boards.
- **Asbestosis** — fibrotic lung disease from chronic asbestos exposure; latency 15-30 yr; restrictive pattern + pleural plaques + calcifications.
- **Mesothelioma** — primary malignancy of pleura (most common) or peritoneum or pericardium; >80% attributable to asbestos exposure; latency 30-50 yr (long-tail). Doll 1955 first established the lung-cancer link; **Selikoff (Mount Sinai, 1964-1979)** prospective cohort of New York insulators conclusively demonstrated mesothelioma + lung cancer + asbestosis exposure-response. Selikoff's work — including the 1964 'Asbestos exposure and neoplasia' conference + 632 insulator deaths analysis — drove asbestos regulation globally.
- **Synergism with tobacco** — Selikoff + Hammond: asbestos + smoking multiplicatively increases lung cancer (RR ~50-90 in smokers + asbestos vs ~5 for asbestos alone or ~10 for smoking alone). Selikoff used this to argue that *individual* asbestos exposure can be assessed only in light of smoking history. Among first demonstrations of true biological synergy in carcinogenesis.
- **Litigation + bans** — asbestos bankruptcies wiped out Johns-Manville (1982), W.R. Grace, Owens Corning, others. >60 countries have banned asbestos; US has banned 'new uses' but legacy asbestos remains widespread.
- **Ongoing global problem** — Russia + India + China + Kazakhstan continue significant chrysotile production + export; Quebec mining ceased 2012.

**Lead (Pb) — occupational**:
- Battery manufacturing + lead smelting + soldering + radiator + ammunition + paint scraping + ship dismantling + e-waste + artisanal gold mining (use of Pb in gold processing in some regions).
- **Carson's Silent Spring (1962)** + Patterson + Needleman + Bellinger established Pb's neurodevelopmental toxicity at population scale.
- Workplace BLL (blood lead level) — OSHA medical removal at >50-60 μg/dL (now widely considered far too permissive given evidence of cardiovascular + cognitive effects at <10 μg/dL).
- Modern occupational Pb burden: battery-recycling workers in LMICs, shooting ranges, certain construction.

**Mercury (Hg) + the Mad Hatter**:
- **'Mad as a hatter'** — 19th-century hat-making used mercury nitrate to mat fur (carroting); chronic Hg vapor exposure → erethism (tremor, irritability, anxiety, memory loss, depression). Idiom predates Lewis Carroll's Hatter (1865); the Hatter's behavior reflected the recognized syndrome.
- Modern occupational Hg: chlor-alkali (now largely phased out); thermometer + thermostat manufacture (declining); dental amalgam (declining); artisanal gold mining (still major global problem — millions of miners exposed; Minamata Convention 2013 targets ASGM).
- Air Hg from coal combustion → global atmospheric Hg → deposition + methylation → fish — broader environmental cycle.

**Vinyl chloride + angiosarcoma** — **John Creech + Maurice Johnson** Goodyear Louisville 1974 — recognized cluster of hepatic angiosarcoma (a rare tumor) in PVC reactor cleaners; led to OSHA emergency standard reducing PEL from 500 ppm to 1 ppm. Classic example of small cluster of rare tumor revealing causal agent.

**Benzene + leukemia** — **Aksoy** Turkish shoemakers (benzene-based adhesives) → AML; **Rinsky NIOSH** Pliofilm cohort cumulative-exposure analysis; Pittsburgh rubber-workers cohort (Wong); IARC Group 1. OSHA PEL lowered to 1 ppm.

These cohort studies + clinical recognitions seeded modern occupational + regulatory toxicology — and most modern OSHA + EPA + IARC frameworks trace back to these workers + the researchers who studied them.

slides.title: Exposure assessment: TLV-TWA, PEL, REL, STEL, biomonitoring, Bradford Hill
slides.body:
**Exposure assessment** = quantifying worker exposure for hazard identification + dose-response + risk management + compliance.

**Occupational exposure limits (OELs)**:

- **TLV (Threshold Limit Value) — ACGIH** (American Conference of Governmental Industrial Hygienists, 1938+): consensus advisory limits, updated annually. Not legally binding (but adopted by reference in many jurisdictions). Three types:
  - **TLV-TWA**: time-weighted average over 8-h workday + 40-h workweek.
  - **TLV-STEL** (Short-Term Exposure Limit): 15-min TWA not to be exceeded.
  - **TLV-C** (Ceiling): instantaneous limit never to be exceeded.

- **PEL (Permissible Exposure Limit) — OSHA** (Occupational Safety and Health Administration, 1971): legally enforceable in US. Most are 1971 PELs adopted from 1968 ACGIH TLVs — many considered outdated. OSHA struggles to update due to procedural + legal hurdles. Some PELs orders of magnitude above modern TLVs.

- **REL (Recommended Exposure Limit) — NIOSH** (National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health, 1970): science-based advisory limits, often more stringent than OSHA PELs. Anchors NIOSH Pocket Guide to Chemical Hazards.

- **EU OEL — SCOEL** + **DNEL (Derived No-Effect Level) under REACH**.

- **Biological Exposure Index (BEI) — ACGIH**: biomonitoring counterpart to TLV; e.g., blood Pb < 30 μg/dL (BEI corresponds to a worker chronically exposed at TLV).

**Bradford Hill criteria** — **Sir Austin Bradford Hill** (1965, Royal Society of Medicine) — nine criteria for causal inference from observational data (developed in the context of smoking + lung cancer, but applied across all of occupational + environmental epidemiology):

1. **Strength of association** — large RR.
2. **Consistency** — replicated across populations + designs.
3. **Specificity** — one cause → one effect (least reliable; many real causes are non-specific).
4. **Temporality** — exposure precedes outcome (the only essential criterion).
5. **Biological gradient (dose-response)** — increasing exposure → increasing risk.
6. **Plausibility** — biological mechanism plausible.
7. **Coherence** — fits other knowledge (epidemiology + lab + clinical).
8. **Experiment** — interventional or natural-experiment evidence.
9. **Analogy** — similar exposures with similar effects.

Not a checklist or scoring system; rather, a framework for weighing evidence. Used in IARC carcinogen evaluations + OSHA + EPA regulatory determinations + Bradford Hill's own work with Richard Doll on smoking + lung cancer (Doll-Hill 1950, 1956, 1976, 1994). Hill: 'all scientific work is incomplete... that does not confer upon us a freedom to ignore the knowledge we already have.'

**Biomonitoring**:
- **Blood + serum + urine** — concentration of parent compound or metabolite reflects internal dose. Blood Pb, urine arsenic, urine cotinine (tobacco), blood Hg, urine cadmium, serum PFAS.
- **Hair + nail** — integrated longer-term exposure; common for Hg (segmental analysis can reconstruct temporal exposure).
- **Adducts** — Hb + albumin + DNA adducts as integrated biomarkers of reactive metabolite exposure (ethylene oxide, acrylamide, aflatoxin — covered in dose-response lesson).
- **CDC NHANES** — National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey biomonitoring program (Calafat, Needham); the gold-standard population reference for chemical exposure in US.
- **EU HBM4EU** — European human biomonitoring initiative (2017-2022).
- **Adapted Bradford Hill in modern practice** — combined with quantitative weight-of-evidence + systematic review (Navigation Guide method; OHAT NTP framework; Cochrane).

**Exposure assessment methods**:
- **Air sampling** — area + personal (lapel sampler with cassette + pump); analytical methods (gravimetric for PM; HPLC + GC-MS for organics; AAS + ICP-MS for metals).
- **Direct-reading instruments** — photoionization detector (PID), flame ionization, IR + electrochemical sensors.
- **Wipe + surface sampling** — for dermal exposure pathway (lead, PCBs, pesticides).
- **Dermal + ingestion estimates** — modeled from contact + transfer + behavior data.
- **Biological monitoring** — as above.
- **Time-activity + task-based modeling** — exposure varies by task; statistical models (NIOSH AHHRA + Bayesian).
- **Personal NIOSH air-sampling + 8-h TWA** — gold standard for compliance with PEL.

**Job-Exposure Matrices (JEMs)** + **CAREX** (Carcinogen Exposure database) — link occupations to exposures for population-level estimation in cohort studies + cancer registry analyses.

**Industrial hygiene practice** — anticipate → recognize → evaluate → control → confirm cycle, as defined by AIHA (American Industrial Hygiene Association).

slides.title: Hazard control hierarchy + PPE + Rana Plaza + abatement
slides.body:
**Hazard control hierarchy** (NIOSH; ANSI Z10) — the foundational framework for occupational hazard reduction, ranked from most to least effective:

1. **Elimination** — remove the hazard entirely (replace with non-hazardous process, automate to remove human contact, eliminate the exposure-producing step).
2. **Substitution** — replace with less hazardous (water-based solvent for toluene, vacuum cleaning for dry sweeping, lead-free solder, asbestos substitutes — fiberglass + mineral wool).
3. **Engineering controls** — physical changes that isolate workers from hazards: enclosed processes, local exhaust ventilation (LEV) with hoods + ducts + filters, isolation booths, robotic remote handling, wet methods for dust suppression, ventilation + dilution.
4. **Administrative controls** — change work practices + behavior: training, work rotation to limit time near hazard, scheduling for low-exposure shifts, signs + labels (GHS — Globally Harmonized System), safety data sheets (SDS), housekeeping, lockout-tagout, hot-work permits, respiratory protection programs.
5. **Personal Protective Equipment (PPE)** — least effective (relies on worker compliance + correct fit + maintenance): respirators (N95, P100, half-face, full-face, PAPR, SCBA), gloves (nitrile, neoprene, butyl rubber by chemical), goggles + face shields, coveralls, hearing protection, fall harnesses.

**Why hierarchy matters**: PPE failures (poor fit, complacency, breakthrough time, fatigue) cause more injuries than engineering-control failures. NIOSH + OSHA require employers to pursue higher-level controls before relying on PPE.

**Respiratory protection**:
- **Filtering facepieces (N95, P100)** — particulate; assigned protection factor (APF) ~10.
- **Half-face + full-face cartridge respirators** — particulate or chemical cartridges; APF 10-50.
- **Powered Air-Purifying Respirator (PAPR)** — APF 25-1000.
- **Supplied-air respirator (SAR) + Self-Contained Breathing Apparatus (SCBA)** — APF 1000-10000; required for IDLH (Immediately Dangerous to Life and Health) atmospheres.
- Fit testing (qualitative + quantitative) required for negative-pressure devices.
- Programs governed by 29 CFR 1910.134.

**Asbestos abatement**:
- Class I-IV work depending on type + amount.
- Containment (negative pressure enclosure with HEPA), wet methods, double-bag disposal, PPE (P100 minimum; PAPR for high-risk), worker training (40-h initial), air monitoring (TEM clearance < 0.01 f/cc).
- EPA + OSHA + state agencies regulate. AHERA (Asbestos Hazard Emergency Response Act, schools).

**Lead abatement** (RRP — Renovation, Repair, and Painting Rule): EPA + HUD certified lead-safe work practices in pre-1978 housing; encapsulation, enclosure, removal options. Worker + child Pb monitoring.

**Confined space + atmosphere testing** — OSHA 1910.146; entry permits, lockout/tagout, air monitoring (O₂, LEL, CO, H₂S), retrieval systems, attendant + entrant + supervisor roles. Confined-space fatalities frequently involve multiple workers (rescuer also dies entering unsafe atmosphere).

**Rana Plaza (2013, Bangladesh)** — garment-factory collapse killed 1134 workers + injured >2500 in Dhaka suburb. Building (originally permitted as commercial, illegally expanded) had visible cracks the day before; workers ordered back. Manufactured clothing for global brands. Catalyzed:
- **Bangladesh Accord on Fire and Building Safety** (2013) — legally binding agreement between brands + unions; 2nd Accord 2018; International Accord 2021. Mandatory inspections + remediation + worker training + complaints.
- **Alliance for Bangladesh Worker Safety** — US-led counterpart.
- **OSHA + global supply-chain attention** — limits of voluntary CSR; need for legally binding worker-rights frameworks.
Not a chemical toxicology case but illustrative of the broader 'occupational safety' frame — chemical hazards + structural + ergonomic + biological + psychosocial together constitute the worker exposome (Wild — covered in modern-frontier lesson).

**Worker rights + global frameworks**:
- **ILO C155 + C170 + C187** — Occupational Safety + Health Conventions.
- **ILO Hazardous Work + Worst Forms of Child Labour**.
- **GHS (Globally Harmonized System of Classification and Labelling of Chemicals)** — adopted globally; pictograms + signal words + hazard statements.
- **Right to Know laws** — OSHA Hazard Communication standard (1983; aligned to GHS in 2012); SDSs available to all workers.
- **EU REACH workplace dimension** — exposure scenarios in extended SDSs.

**Worker compensation + occupational disease registries** — vary by jurisdiction; OSHA recordable injury + illness logs; BLS Survey of Occupational Injuries and Illnesses; SENSOR (NIOSH state-based surveillance); occupational disease often under-recognized + under-compensated due to long latency + multifactorial causation.

question.question: Investigate suspected silicosis in an engineered-stone fabricator
question.goal: A 32-yr-old man presenting with progressive dyspnea has worked for 8 years cutting + finishing engineered-stone (quartz) countertops in a small shop without ventilation or respiratory protection. Chest CT shows upper-lobe nodules + early progressive massive fibrosis. Walk through diagnosis + exposure assessment + remediation.

steps.prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis + the agent?

acceptedAnswers: accelerated silicosis from engineered-stone (quartz, ~93% silica) fabrication

steps.reveal: Accelerated silicosis. Engineered-stone countertops are ~93% silica (vs ~30% in granite, <5% in marble); dry cutting + grinding generates very high respirable crystalline silica (RCS) exposure. Workers develop silicosis 10-15× faster than traditional stone workers — accelerated form (5-10 yr latency) increasingly common. First described as an epidemic in Israel (2010, Kramer + Bar-Ziv), Spain, Australia; now widespread including Texas + California (Hua + Rose 2019). Many cases are young (<40), with severe + progressive disease + cor pulmonale + lung transplant or death.

acceptedAnswers: personal air sampling for RCS over 8-h TWA + observe processes + interview workers + check ventilation + PPE

steps.reveal: Industrial hygiene investigation: (1) personal 8-h TWA RCS sampling (NIOSH 7500 method, X-ray diffraction analysis) per OSHA standard at PEL 50 μg/m³; engineered-stone fabricators frequently exceed PEL 10-100×; (2) area sampling near workstations; (3) walkthrough — wet vs dry methods, LEV (local exhaust ventilation), respirator program, housekeeping; (4) interview workers — symptoms, history, prior employers, tobacco; (5) review medical surveillance records (chest x-ray ILO B-readings, spirometry); (6) tuberculin testing (silicotuberculosis risk). OSHA enforcement + NIOSH HHE (Health Hazard Evaluation) possible.

acceptedAnswers: elimination/substitution then engineering (wet methods + LEV) then administrative then PPE respirators

steps.reveal: Hazard control hierarchy applied: (1) **Elimination/substitution** — switch to porcelain or natural stone (lower silica); difficult given customer demand; engineered-stone companies developing lower-silica alternatives (e.g., Caesarstone Mineral). (2) **Engineering** — mandatory **wet-cutting + wet-grinding + wet-polishing**; **local exhaust ventilation** at all dry processes if any; HEPA-filtered vacuum cleaning; enclosed workstations. (3) **Administrative** — training; medical surveillance (spirometry + low-dose CT yearly for chronic exposed); rotation; signage; tobacco cessation (synergism). (4) **PPE** — properly fit-tested respirators (P100; PAPR for higher exposures); skin/clothing protection; shower + change-room. **Australia banned engineered stone** entirely from July 2024 — first national ban + the most aggressive elimination response. California + several states issued emergency silica standards.

acceptedAnswers: remove from exposure + supportive care + lung transplant evaluation + screen co-workers

steps.reveal: Medical management: (1) remove from exposure permanently; (2) supportive care (bronchodilators if airflow obstruction, oxygen, pulmonary rehab); (3) treat any superimposed TB; (4) lung-transplant evaluation if progressive; (5) workers' compensation claim + ATS/ERS clinical guidelines. **Cohort response**: screen all co-workers (chest x-ray B-read, spirometry) — silica + silicosis is an occupational disease cluster requiring investigation of the shop + similar shops + the supply chain. Notify OSHA + state public-health authorities (silicosis is a reportable disease in many states; SENSOR-Silicosis NIOSH surveillance). Selikoff-style cohort epidemiology in the engineered-stone industry now underway in multiple countries.

question.question: Why is the hazard-control hierarchy (elimination > substitution > engineering > administrative > PPE) the foundational principle of industrial hygiene?
options: Because higher-level controls (elimination, substitution, engineering) are more effective + reliable than lower-level controls (administrative, PPE) — they don't depend on consistent worker behavior, training, fit, or maintenance. PPE failures (improper fit, compliance lapses, breakthrough time) cause more injuries than engineering-control failures. NIOSH + OSHA require employers to pursue higher-level controls first, treating PPE as a last resort + supplement rather than primary defense.
question.explanation: Hazard-control hierarchy (NIOSH; ANSI Z10) is ranked by effectiveness + reliability: **Elimination** > **Substitution** > **Engineering controls** > **Administrative controls** > **PPE**. Higher levels physically separate workers from hazards, requiring no continuous behavior compliance; lower levels (administrative, PPE) depend on consistent worker action + maintenance. PPE has well-documented failure modes: poor fit (especially with facial hair, women's faces sized for men's respirators), compliance lapses (uncomfortable, hot, restrictive), breakthrough time (chemical cartridges have finite lifespan), incorrect selection (wrong cartridge for the chemical), fatigue + complacency, training gaps. **NIOSH + OSHA require employers to demonstrate that higher-level controls are infeasible before relying on PPE**. Real-world examples: dry-sweeping replaced by wet-method (engineering); leaded gasoline phased out (elimination); local exhaust ventilation rather than respirators; automated dipping rather than manual immersion. Modern Industry 4.0 + robotics moves further toward elimination by automating exposure-producing tasks. The COVID-19 pandemic re-emphasized hierarchy: ventilation + air filtration (engineering) > masking (PPE) > distancing (administrative).

hints: Why aren't all controls equally effective?
slides.workedSolution: Hierarchy ranks effectiveness: elimination > substitution > engineering > administrative > PPE. Higher levels remove hazard physically + don't depend on worker compliance; lower levels (especially PPE) have failure modes (poor fit, compliance, breakthrough). NIOSH + OSHA require pursuing higher levels first. PPE is supplement + last resort, not primary defense.

question.question: Designing an occupational toxicology programme for a battery-recycling facility
question.prompt: You are a corporate industrial hygienist at a lead-acid battery recycling plant in a US state. Process: smelter melts crushed batteries; refining; casting ingots. Workers handle lead dust + lead oxide + sulfuric acid mist. Current PEL: OSHA 50 μg/m³ Pb. Discuss: (a) the exposure pathways (inhalation of Pb fume + dust; dermal + ingestion via hand-to-mouth; take-home contamination of family members on clothing); (b) the medical surveillance you would implement (baseline + 6-monthly BLL, ZPP, hematology, kidney function, semen analysis for younger workers); (c) hazard-control hierarchy applied (mechanized + enclosed processes; LEV with HEPA; wet methods; lower-PEL substitution where possible — e.g., automated robotic handling; admin controls: rotation, training, hygiene; PPE: P100 respirators, washable clothing/shoes left at work, shower-in-shower-out, separate canteen); (d) family + community concerns (Pb-contaminated take-home dust on clothing; perimeter Pb in soil; ATSDR Health Assessment for nearby residents); (e) regulatory landscape (OSHA Lead standard 1910.1025 — likely to be lowered; CDC/NIOSH BLL reference values; state-specific Pb registries; ACGIH BEI); (f) Bradford Hill applied — how to evaluate suggestive findings (e.g., elevated hypertension in workers) given multiple cohorts + decades of evidence; (g) Rana Plaza lessons + global frameworks — Pb-recycling in LMICs (informal sector + child labor) + transboundary battery waste.

question.question: A worker is exposed for 4 hours at 200 μg/m³ + 4 hours at 30 μg/m³ for an 8-h day. What is the 8-h TWA exposure in μg/m³ (compare to OSHA silica PEL of 50 μg/m³)?

question.prompt: In ≤120 words, explain how Selikoff (asbestos), Doll-Hill (smoking + Bradford Hill criteria), Hawks Nest (silica), Aksoy + Rinsky (benzene), Creech + Johnson (vinyl chloride), + Rana Plaza shaped modern occupational toxicology + worker-safety frameworks.
question.rubric: Mentions: Selikoff Mount Sinai insulator cohort (1964-1979) → asbestos-mesothelioma-lung cancer exposure-response + tobacco synergism; Doll + Hill 1950+1976+1994 + Austin Bradford Hill criteria (1965) for causal inference; Hawks Nest tunnel disaster 1930-1932 + acute silicosis + OSHA silica standard 2016 + engineered-stone resurgence; Aksoy Turkish shoemakers + Rinsky NIOSH Pliofilm cohort for benzene-AML; Creech + Johnson Goodyear 1974 vinyl chloride-angiosarcoma → OSHA emergency standard; Rana Plaza 2013 → Bangladesh Accord + supply-chain accountability; together drove (1) PEL + TLV + REL exposure-limit framework; (2) NIOSH-OSHA hazard-control hierarchy elimination > substitution > engineering > admin > PPE; (3) Bradford Hill causal-inference framework; (4) biomonitoring + BEI + CDC NHANES + EU HBM4EU; (5) GHS + Hazard Communication + worker right-to-know; (6) global ILO + ILO C155 OSH framework. Concludes: occupational toxicology pioneered methods + frameworks now used across all of environmental + regulatory toxicology.
